newsitem.title: GUAM: Frantic search for survivors of Guam air crash.
newsitem.headline: Frantic search for survivors of Guam air crash.

text.p: Rescue workers searched frantically for survivors from the Korean jumbo jet which crashed in Guam on Wednesday, eyewitnesses said.

Hours after the airliner crashed on a hillside seven miles (12 km) south of the U.S. territory's airport, the search was extended to surrounding areas to look for people who may have been flung out by the impact.
"We are continuing to go to the wreckage site to make sure that there is no one we are not able to find," a spokeswoman for Guam governor Carl Gutierrez said.
An eyewitness said he saw several body bags in the area, which was swarming with rescue teams comprising military personnel as well as Red Cross members and private citizens.

Andrew Murphy, spokesman for the Guam Airport Authority, said the number of survivors taken to hospital had risen to 35. He declined to comment on a Korean Air Lines official's statement that at least 55 people may have survived.
"The figures we know as of now are of people in hospital and we know for certain are alive," another official said.
Governor Gutierrez said more than 200 of the 254 people on board the flight died in the crash.
Eyewitnesses said the crash impact split the aircraft into five parts and it was miraculous that some people managed to escape from the burning wreckage.

"I saw some people were able to walk away from the wreckage. The plane was in five pieces and it's a miracle that anyone could come out of this," said Dr Michael Lancer, a Guam resident who reached the wreckage while it was still burning.
The aircraft, flying from Seoul to Guam, was carrying 225 adults, three children, three infants and 23 crew members.
After the night-time crash, rescuers used floodlights to illuminate the site, located in rough terrain in a sparsely populated area called Nimitz.
As dawn broke over the Pacific island territory, the search continued. What appeared to be a wing and other fragments of wreckage were silhouetted against the trees on the hillside.
Rescuers said the grass in the area, up to five feet (1.7 metres) tall, and the rains at night made movement extremely difficult.
Governor Gutierrez, who lives nearby and was among the first to reach the wreckage, said he had rescued five people from the airliner.

Gutierrez said he was told by survivor Barry Small of New Zealand, a helicopter pilot and mechanic, who was sitting in row 13 of the plane that there were no indications of trouble in mid-flight or during the approach to the landing.
Gutierrez said the plane had caught fire after it hit an oil pipeline that runs through the jungle area that islanders call the "boondocks" just outside the capital.
Rear Admiral Martin Janzack, the top Navy official in Guam, said the two flight recorders had been found and sent to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in Honolulu, Hawaii.
